title: Thinking in loops: Inkling 2 Mini, Dory and latent reasoning
summary: Looped transformers reuse the same layers several times per token, trading chain-of-thought tokens for hidden computation, and Inkling 2 Mini and NVIDIA's Dory are the first serious open models built this way. We explain the mechanism, the cost and caching trade-offs, what it means for monitorability, and how to test whether a local looped model beats a dense one on your own tasks.
shownotes:
The mechanism: a sandwich of input block, shared recurrent block and output block; Inkling 2 Mini runs 24 stored layers as 48, Dory runs 72 layers as 32 + 40k
Making loops trainable: Inkling's closed-start learned gate, Dory's input re-injection on a normalised transformer, sampled loop counts and truncated backprop for elastic depth
Where to loop and what it buys: middle-layer looping beats last-layer looping; looping improves reasoning, coding and agentic tasks but not stored knowledge, so pair it with retrieval
The cost maths: more loops, fewer tokens and turns; Dory at two loops costs 1.03-1.25x one loop but recovers most of the four-loop gain; measure cost per solved task
The serving catch: per-loop KV caches, last-loop caching, self-speculative decoding, quantisation-aware distillation and young local runtime support
Monitorability: no-CoT time horizon rises from 16 to 37 seconds, but LinuxArena stealth shows no clear trend at this scale
This week: a local bake-off of Inkling 2 Mini or Dory at two loops against your current dense model, with Dutch inputs tested separately, capped turns and a sandbox
